title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Real estate portfolio management
audience: Owners of small Australian property management businesses who need an hourly rate for ad hoc work and a minimum charge for single visits, before quoting.
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill for portfolio work.
Calculate a base hourly rate for ad hoc portfolio work from the owner's own costs and income target. No fee or hourly benchmark for portfolio management was found, so none is used.
Set a minimum charge for single visits and short tasks, and explain it to an owner before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A portfolio rate depends on the skill and reliability of the work, experience, how scarce good management is locally, the range of services an owner can buy in one place (routine management, inspections, tenancy events, maintenance coordination, and reporting), and the cost of running the business. A manager who handles the whole tenancy cycle may justify a higher rate, because the owner saves several separate providers. A new business should price honestly and review the rate regularly, rather than cut it to win work. The research for this course found no hourly or monthly management fee for any state, so the base rate must come from the owner's own costs and billable hours, and any monthly fee must be built from them.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between properties, quoting, owner calls, admin, marketing, training, software upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours, which is a general range and not an Australian property management figure (Jobber, What are billable hours, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026). If only 60 of every 100 paid hours can be billed, the costs of all 100 hours must come out of the 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week. Check your own log against the range.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, vehicle, software, trust administration, professional fees, phone, marketing, accounting and any licence fees, to the income you need. Business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each will be allowed for (Choose a pricing strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026). A registered tax agent should confirm how leave and superannuation are treated for your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by the billable hours to reach the base rate. An Australian personal-training guide works backwards from a target income, dividing by working weeks and then weekly hours, with tax and costs added on top (AIPT, 16 May 2025). Its example figures are not used here. Review the base rate each quarter.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for single visits
instruction.body: A single property visit, such as a one-off inspection or a key handover, can cost more in time than it earns, because travel, set-up, reporting and cleanup do not shrink with the size of the visit. A minimum charge or call-out fee covers the visit. No minimum charge or call-out fee for property management was found in the research, so the figure must come from your own costs. A contractor guide suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, setup and cleanup. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). State the minimum before the visit, and explain it to the owner in plain terms.

instruction.heading: Reviewing and raising rates
instruction.body: Business Victoria recommends reviewing prices about every three months, to check that they still suit the business and its customers (Develop a pricing strategy, no date shown on the page). Raise rates at least once a year to allow for cost and market change. Give existing owners notice of a new rate, and honour appointments already agreed at the old rate. Competitor rates are a guide, not a target. Compare only with licensed, insured managers, because licences, insurance and costs differ.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, vehicle, software, trust administration, phone and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and reporting for a single visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: A manager plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed. The manager's log for one month (hypothetical, for this lesson) shows that about 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: If costs and income are divided by all paid hours, the rate looks lower than it should, because the costs still have to come out of the 60 billable hours. The manager builds the rate from billable hours, checks the minimum charge, and then publishes it with a review date. No hourly or monthly management benchmark is available to compare it with, so the manager relies on the business's own records. The factor of about 1.67 is arithmetic from the hypothetical log (100 divided by 60). It is not a sourced figure.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month, with the property and the task
Price sheet with the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a competitor's figure, or from a general guide, without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking single visits at the hourly rate, without covering travel and setup.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, setup and reporting.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (ACCC, Setting prices: what's allowed, last modified 15 July 2026). That page does not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a fee schedule.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave and superannuation with a registered tax agent before the rate is published. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Letting property and collecting rent for others for reward can need a licence. In Queensland, real estate agent licences and resident letting agent licences cover this (Property Occupations Act 2014, sections 26 and 27; excerpt read only). Victorian residential rental manager licensing was not verified. Check the rule for each state before publishing a fee schedule for that work.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any single visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for single visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: A manager can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and the owner pays less
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average on a website and the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a single property visit?
options: Because a single visit needs travel but no set-up or reporting at all
Because travel, set-up and reporting time does not shrink with the size of the visit
Because owners expect every visit to cost the same amount, whatever it involves
Because a minimum charge replaces a written appointment for every property

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate for portfolio work?
options: A single fee quoted on a competitor's website, with no check of its costs
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a listing site this week

No property management hourly rate, monthly fee or minimum charge was found in the sources read for this course: UNCONFIRMED.
